title: When should you use AQE skew handling vs manual salting — AQE is the first thing to try (automatic, no code change), but if AQE doesn't sufficiently address the skew (both sides skewed on same key, or non-join skew like groupBy), salting or isolate-and-broadcast the hot keys may be needed?
shortTitle: When to use AQE skew handling vs manual salting

s1_definition.profdef: Adaptive Query Execution's skew join optimization should be your first choice because it detects oversized shuffle partitions at runtime and automatically splits them into smaller sub-partitions with no code change, handling the common case of a single skewed join side. You fall back to manual techniques — salting or isolating and broadcasting the hot keys — when AQE is insufficient, such as when both sides are skewed on the same key, when the skew is in a non-join operation like a groupBy that AQE's skew-join logic does not cover, or when you need finer control than AQE's automatic thresholds provide.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, AQE skew handling is like an automatic supervisor who, mid-shift, notices one clerk is buried and quietly splits that clerk's pile among several helpers — no change to your instructions needed. You only step in manually, with salting or by pulling the mega-account aside for special handling, when the automatic supervisor cannot cope: when the overload exists on both lists at once, or when the overload is in a totalling task rather than a matching task, which is outside the supervisor's remit.
s1_definition.oneliner: Try AQE skew handling first because it is automatic and code-free; use salting or isolate-and-broadcast when AQE cannot cope — both sides skewed, groupBy skew, or when you need manual control.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Adaptive Query Execution's skew join optimization should be your first choice because it detects oversized shuffle partitions at runtime and automatically splits them into smaller sub-partitions with no code change, handling the common case of a single skewed join side. You fall back to manual techniques — salting or isolating and broadcasting the hot keys — when AQE is insufficient, such as when both sides are skewed on the same key, when the skew is in a non-join operation like a groupBy that AQE's skew-join logic does not cover, or when you need finer control than AQE's automatic thresholds provide.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India, AQE skew handling is like an automatic supervisor who, mid-shift, notices one clerk is buried and quietly splits that clerk's pile among several helpers — no change to your instructions needed. You only step in manually, with salting or by pulling the mega-account aside for special handling, when the automatic supervisor cannot cope: when the overload exists on both lists at once, or when the overload is in a totalling task rather than a matching task, which is outside the supervisor's remit.

**One line to remember:** Try AQE skew handling first because it is automatic and code-free; use salting or isolate-and-broadcast when AQE cannot cope — both sides skewed, groupBy skew, or when you need manual control.

sections.s2_technical:
AQE skew handling is the default modern approach. With Adaptive Query Execution enabled and its skew-join setting on, Spark measures the actual size of each shuffle partition at the stage boundary. If a partition is much larger than the median — governed by a skewed-partition factor and an absolute byte threshold — AQE splits that partition into several smaller sub-partitions and, on a sort-merge join, replicates the matching partition on the other side so the split sub-partitions still find their matches. The big advantage is that it requires no code change: you enable the configuration and Spark adapts at runtime using real statistics, which also means it catches skew that only appears as data grows.

AQE works best for the common case: one side of a join skewed on a key. It splits the oversized partition and balances the work automatically. But it has limits. When both sides are heavily skewed on the same key, splitting one side and replicating the other can itself blow up, and AQE's automatic handling may not fully resolve it. When the skew is not in a join but in a groupBy or other aggregation, AQE's skew-join optimization does not apply, because it is specifically a join optimization. And AQE's decisions are driven by thresholds, so an unusual distribution may fall outside what the thresholds catch, leaving residual skew.

Manual salting is the fallback for these cases. As covered in the salting technique, you append a random salt to the hot key to spread it across partitions and replicate the other side to preserve matches, and for a skewed groupBy you do a two-stage aggregation — aggregate per salted key, then re-aggregate across salts. Salting gives you precise control over how the hot key is spread, which is what you need when AQE's automatic logic is insufficient.

Isolate-and-broadcast is another manual fallback. You split the join into two parts: filter out the few hot keys and join them separately using a broadcast join (because the hot keys' rows on the small side are tiny and broadcasting avoids shuffling the huge hot partition), while the remaining cold keys go through a normal join. You then union the two results. This directly removes the hot key from the shuffle path. It works well when the hot keys are few and known.

A senior-level nuance is the decision order and combining techniques. The practical workflow is: first ensure AQE and its skew-join setting are enabled and let it try; inspect the Spark UI to confirm whether stragglers remain; if skew persists, identify the hot keys by profiling; then choose salting for groupBy skew or both-sides skew, or isolate-and-broadcast when the hot keys are few. You can also tune AQE's skew thresholds before resorting to code. The goal is to prefer the zero-code automatic path and only add intrusive, maintained code when the data genuinely requires it.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India has a transactions-to-accounts join skewed on one pooling account. AQE skew handling splits the oversized partition automatically and resolves it with no code change. This is the AQE-sufficient case.

Problem 2 — A different job groups transactions by account id to compute totals, and the same pooling account skews the groupBy. AQE's skew-join optimization does not cover groupBy, so stragglers remain. This needs salting with two-stage aggregation.

Problem 3 — A join is skewed on a handful of known mega-accounts. Isolating those few hot keys and broadcasting their small-side rows, then unioning with the cold-key join, removes the skew cleanly. This is isolate-and-broadcast.

The demo takes a skew situation described by whether it is a join or groupBy, whether both sides are skewed, and how many hot keys there are, and recommends AQE, salting, or isolate-and-broadcast, logging the reasoning.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: five skew situations differing by operation, whether both sides are skewed, and the number of hot keys.

Step 1: For the transactions-to-accounts join with a single hot account, the advisor sees a join, one side skewed, and no special condition, so it recommends AQE skew join — the automatic, no-code path to try first.

Step 2: For the groupBy totals skewed by the hot account, the advisor recognizes that AQE's skew-join optimization does not cover groupBy, so it recommends salting with a two-stage aggregation.

Step 3: For the join where both sides are skewed on the same key, the advisor knows AQE's split-and-replicate can blow up, so it recommends salting.

Step 4: For the join with three known mega-accounts, the advisor sees a small number of hot keys and recommends isolate-and-broadcast — handle those three separately with a broadcast join and union with the cold-key join.

Step 5: For the join with many moderate keys and no distinct hot key, it defaults to AQE skew join. The demo logs each recommendation and the overall escalation order.

sections.s6_takeaway:
My first move for skew is always Adaptive Query Execution's skew join optimization, because it is automatic and requires no code change. With AQE and its skew-join setting enabled, Spark measures the actual size of each shuffle partition at the stage boundary, and when a partition is much larger than the median — judged by a skewed-partition factor and an absolute byte threshold — it splits that partition into smaller sub-partitions and, on a sort-merge join, replicates the matching side so the splits still find their matches. Because it uses real runtime statistics, it also catches skew that only emerges as data grows, and it handles the common case of a single join side skewed on a key very well.

I escalate to manual techniques only when AQE is insufficient, and there are three clear cases. First, when the skew is in a groupBy or other aggregation rather than a join, AQE's skew-join logic does not apply, so I use salting with a two-stage aggregation — aggregate per salted key, then re-aggregate across salts for the true total. Second, when both sides are skewed on the same key, AQE's split-and-replicate approach can itself blow up, so salting with careful control is safer. Third, when there are a few known hot keys, I isolate and broadcast them — filter those keys out, join them separately with a broadcast join because their small-side rows are tiny, and union the result with the normal join of the cold keys, which removes the hot key from the shuffle path entirely.

At the National Bank of India this was the exact playbook. A transactions-to-accounts join skewed on one pooling account was resolved just by enabling AQE skew join, with no code change. But a per-account groupBy skewed by the same account needed salting with a two-stage aggregation because AQE did not cover it, and a join skewed on a handful of corporate mega-accounts was cleanest with isolate-and-broadcast. The workflow I describe in interviews is to enable AQE skew join first, confirm in the Spark UI whether stragglers remain, profile to find the hot keys if they do, tune AQE's thresholds as a next step, and only then add the intrusive salting or isolate-and-broadcast code — preferring the zero-code automatic path and reaching for manual control only when the data genuinely requires it.
